chunks.arabic_text: ١١ - سَهْلُ بْنُ زِيَادٍ، أَبُو سَعِيدٍ، الْآدَمِيُّ، الرَّازِيُّ.

translations.en: 11 – Sahl ibn Ziyād, Abū Saʿīd, al-Ādamī, al-Rāzī.

chunks.arabic_text: كَانَ ضَعِيفًا جِدًّا، فَاسِدَ الرِّوَايَةِ وَالدِّينِ. وَكَانَ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عِيسَى الْأَشْعَرِيُّ أَخْرَجَهُ مِنْ قُمٍ، وَأَظْهَرَ الْبَرَاءَةَ مِنْهُ، وَنَهَى النَّاسَ عَنِ السَّمَاعِ مِنْهُ وَالرِّوَايَةَ عَنْهُ. وَيَرْوِي الْمَرَاسِيلَ، وَيَعْتَمِدُ الْمَجَاهِيلَ.

translations.en: He was very weak, corrupt in narration and religion. Aḍmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Ashʿarī exiled him from Qum, declared barā’a from him, and forbade the people from listening to him and narrating from him. He narrates mursal narrations and depends on unknown people.

en.summary: This entry from al-Ghada'iri's *Kitab al-Du'afa* highlights the rigorous scrutiny applied to narrators in the Shia scholarly tradition, specifically targeting Sahl ibn Ziyād for his weak memory and religious integrity. Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa al-Ash'ari’s public disassociation (*al-Bara'ah*) and exile of Sahl from Qum underscore the importance of reliable transmission chains (*isnad*) in preserving authentic hadith. His reliance on *mursal* narrations and unknown figures further illustrates the criteria used to distinguish between trustworthy and weak sources in early Shia hadith sciences.
en.seo_question: Who was Sahl ibn Ziyād and why was he considered a weak narrator?
